# Part 1 — The REAAAPP Workflow {background-color="#1A1A1A"}

Read · Explore · Assume · Apply · Assess · Present · Publish

## Why You Need a Workflow

::: {.goal}
Analysis fails more often from missing process than from missing statistics.
:::

- Data arrive bigger, in more formats, and from more centres than before
- Analyses are more complex, so more places to go quietly wrong
- Without a named sequence, steps get skipped under time pressure
- A shared workflow lets a team divide work without losing the thread
- Reviewers and journals increasingly ask how, not just what

## REAAAPP at a Glance

| | Stage | What it delivers |
|---|---|---|
| **R** | Read | Data of known provenance, in your environment |
| **E** | Explore | Understanding of distribution, missingness, structure |
| **A** | Assume | An explicit list of what the analysis depends on |
| **A** | Apply | Fitted models and methods |
| **A** | Assess | Evidence the model is adequate and valid |
| **P** | Present | Results an audience can act on |
| **P** | Publish | Results, data and code others can verify |

## How Each Stage Is Presented

Every stage in this part gets the same two slides.

- **Goal** — what the stage must achieve before you move on
- **Knowledge required** — what you need to understand
- **Skill required** — what you need to be able to do
- **Tools** — what you do it with
- Learn the shape once, then read any stage quickly

## R — Read Data

::: {.goal}
**Goal:** get the data into R with its provenance, types and missing-value
conventions intact.
:::

- Sources are offline, cloud, or hybrid — record which
- Structured formats: CSV, Excel, SPSS, SAS, Stata
- Unstructured sources need a conversion step you must document
- Reading is where silent type coercion does its damage
- Nothing downstream is trustworthy if this step is careless

## R — Read: Knowledge and Skill

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Knowledge required
- How your source format encodes missing values
- Variable types and what coercion costs you
- Where the data came from and who owns it
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Skill required
- Import with `readr`, `haven`, `readxl`
- Script the import and check types — never edit the raw file
:::
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Tools: readr · haven · readxl · here
:::

## E — Explore Data

::: {.goal}
**Goal:** understand distributions, missingness and structure before any model
is fitted.
:::

- Exploration takes two forms: visualisation and tabulation
- EDA summarises the main characteristics of the data
- This is the stage most often skipped, and it costs the most
- Impossible values and implausible ranges surface here or not at all
- Missingness has a pattern — find out what it is

## E — Explore: Knowledge and Skill

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Knowledge required
- What EDA is for, and when you have done enough
- When a graphic beats a table, and when it does not
- What a missingness pattern implies for the analysis
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Skill required
- Summarise with `skimr` and `gtsummary`, plot with `ggplot2`
- Read a distribution and spot impossible values
:::
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Tools: ggplot2 · gtsummary · skimr · naniar
:::

## A — Assume

::: {.goal}
**Goal:** state what the intended analysis depends on, before fitting it.
:::

- Every statistical test carries underlying assumptions
- Statistics does not infer valid conclusions from nothing
- The sample must be representative of the population you claim to describe
- Name the roles: exposure, confounder, mediator, moderator
- State the outcome and the relationship you assume it has

## A — Assume: Knowledge and Skill

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Knowledge required
- Population versus sample, and what representativeness buys you
- Exposure, confounder, mediator and moderator are different roles
- Outcome types: continuous, binary, count, time-to-event
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Skill required
- Draw the assumed relationship before you fit anything
- Write the assumptions down where a reviewer can read them
:::
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Tools: DAGitty · dagitty · a whiteboard and a photograph of it
:::

## A — Apply Models and Methods

::: {.goal}
**Goal:** fit the models and methods the research question actually needs.
:::

- Statistical analysis covers estimation, hypothesis testing, inference and prediction
- Decide first whether you want inference or prediction — they are not the same
- Univariable before multivariable; univariate is not multivariate
- Machine learning adds supervised, unsupervised and semi-supervised work
- R is the working environment: a language plus a runtime for all of it

## A — Apply: Knowledge and Skill

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Knowledge required
- Estimation, testing, inference and prediction are distinct goals
- Univariable versus multivariable model building
- Where statistical learning ends and machine learning begins
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Skill required
- Fit with `lm`, `glm` and `lme4`, and read the output
- Keep every model in a script that runs start to finish
:::
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Tools: R · RStudio · Posit Cloud · lm · glm · lme4 · tidymodels
:::

## A — Assess Results and Models

::: {.goal}
**Goal:** show that the model is adequate, and say where the result applies.
:::

- Re-check the assumptions against the model you actually fitted
- Outliers and influential observations are two different problems
- Performance for continuous outcomes: R-squared and residual behaviour
- Performance for classification: accuracy, sensitivity, specificity
- Validity: internal first, then how far the result travels

## A — Assess: Knowledge and Skill

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Knowledge required
- What diagnostic plots can and cannot tell you
- The difference between an outlier and an influential point
- Internal versus external validity
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Skill required
- Read diagnostic output and compute the right performance measure
- Decide when to revise the model and when to stop
:::
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Tools: broom · performance · car · pROC
:::

## P — Present Results

::: {.goal}
**Goal:** report the results so that the audience can act on them.
:::

- Reporting guidelines exist: SAMPL covers basic statistical reporting
- The ASA is explicit — no single index should substitute for scientific reasoning
- Report the estimate and its precision, not the p-value alone
- Find out what your audience already understands before you simplify
- Simplifying and convincing are part of the analysis, not an afterthought

## P — Present: Knowledge and Skill

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Knowledge required
- The SAMPL guidelines for biomedical journals
- The ASA statement on p-values and statistical significance
- What your audience already knows and what they need
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Skill required
- Build tables with `gtsummary` and `gt`
- Write an interpretation, not just an estimate
:::
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Tools: gtsummary · gt · flextable · Quarto
:::

## P — Publish Results, Data and Code

::: {.goal}
**Goal:** release results, data and code so that others can verify them.
:::

- Code belongs in version control in the cloud, not in a folder on your laptop
- GitHub adds access control, issue tracking and continuous integration to Git
- Data can be deposited in Zenodo, OSF, Dryad, figshare or a domain repository
- Results can be published as a site, a report, or a dashboard
- Shiny turns an analysis into something a clinician can actually use

## P — Publish: Knowledge and Skill

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Knowledge required
- What version control does that careful file naming does not
- Repository and licence choices for data
- What makes a dataset reusable by someone who was not there
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.ks}
### Skill required
- Use Git and GitHub for code, results and reports
- Deposit the data and publish a Quarto site or a Shiny app
:::
:::
::::

::: {.note}
Tools: Git · GitHub · Quarto · Shiny · Zenodo · OSF · Dryad
:::

## Reproducibility Runs Through Every Stage

::: {.goal}
Every stage should leave behind an artefact that someone else can rerun.
:::

- The raw file is read-only; every change to it happens in code
- Relative paths, so the project survives moving between machines
- Record package versions — results drift when packages change

```r
library(here)
library(readr)

dat_raw <- read_csv(here("data-raw", "cohort_2026.csv"))
```

## Working in a Team: Git as the Backbone

::: {.goal}
Analysis by a team means code, results and reports have to move together.
:::

- Git records who changed what and when, without renamed copies
- Cloud drives sync files; only a commit records why the change was made
- Branches let two analysts work without overwriting each other

```bash
git add analysis/model-fit.R
git commit -m "Fit adjusted model with centre as random intercept"
git push
```

## Reporting Guidelines You Should Know

- **SAMPL** — Statistical Analyses and Methods in the Published Literature
- **ASA statement on p-values**, *The American Statistician*, 2016
- **AHA/ASA** statistical reporting recommendations for cardiovascular research
- The EQUATOR Network hosts these alongside the study-design checklists
- Read the guideline for your design before you write the methods section

## Publishing Data: Credit and Reuse

::: {.goal}
A deposited dataset is a citable research output in its own right.
:::

- Credit and recognition for work that a paper alone does not show
- Discoverability — indexed repositories reach readers your paper will not
- Reusability and accessibility for the next research question
- Zenodo, OSF, Dryad and figshare; GEO and GenBank for domain data

## Rate Yourself at Each Stage

::: {.goal}
Ask two questions at every stage: am I using the right tools, and how good am I
with them?
:::

- **Novice** — you can follow a worked example
- **Intermediate** — you can adapt it to your own data
- **Advanced** — you can judge when the method itself is wrong
- The gaps are rarely uniform; rate yourself stage by stage
- Where the gap matters, get trained or bring in a collaborator

## Where Workflows Break Down

- Explore is skipped when the deadline is close, and the errors surface late
- Assumptions stay in your head, so nobody can check them
- Models are fitted but never assessed
- Analyses are finished but never published, so nothing can be verified
- No version control, so `final_v3_really_final.R` becomes the archive

## Part 1 — Recap

::: {.goal}
Read · Explore · Assume · Apply · Assess · Present · Publish
:::

- Data arrive in many formats and analyses keep getting more complex
- Use the right tools at each stage, and know how good you are with them
- Knowledge and skill are different things; each stage needs both
- Work in a team and leverage other people's expertise
- Be willing to let go of the old tools
